text: Last lesson's subquery had to return exactly one value. This lesson relaxes that rule completely — subqueries that return a whole list, used with IN.

Remember IN with a hard-coded list from Lesson 15? Where subcategory ID in 1, 2, 3. That works, but it's frozen at the exact moment you wrote it. Add or remove a subcategory, and this list silently stops matching reality.

The fix: put a subquery where that hard-coded list used to be. Where subcategory ID IN, open paren, select subcategory ID from ProductSubcategory where name starts with Mountain, close paren. Instead of frozen numbers, the inner query GENERATES the list dynamically, every time it runs. As the data changes, this stays correct automatically — read it as plain English: where this ID is IN the set of values that inner query returns. And unlike last lesson's scalar subquery, this one can return any number of rows at all — IN is built specifically to handle a list.

NOT IN works the same basic way, but it has a serious, silent trap. If the subquery's results contain even ONE NULL, the entire NOT IN comparison returns zero rows — no error, no warning, just silently wrong. This traces straight back to Lesson 16: NULL means unknown, and asking 'is this NOT equal to unknown' can never resolve to true. The safer fix, which we'll cover properly in Lesson 55, is NOT EXISTS instead of NOT IN whenever NULL is even a possibility.

IN with a subquery generates a dynamic list instead of a frozen one; NOT IN carries a real NULL trap worth remembering. Next lesson: correlated subqueries, which reference the outer query row by row. See you there.
